text: FIDO2 and passkeys replace the password-plus-code model with public-key cryptography. This lesson covers what the standard actually does, why it's genuinely phishing-resistant rather than just another factor, what a passkey is in everyday terms, and why both are considered stronger than the SMS and push-based MFA covered earlier in this chapter.

When you register a FIDO2 credential, your device generates a key pair. The private key never leaves the device, often protected behind a PIN, fingerprint, or face scan. The public key goes to the site, and on its own it's useless to an attacker. To log in, the site sends a challenge and your device signs it with the private key, proving possession without ever transmitting the key itself — there's no shared secret sitting on a server to steal in bulk.

The property that makes FIDO2 phishing-resistant is origin binding. The credential is cryptographically tied to the exact domain it was registered for, such as login.realbank.com. Land on a convincing lookalike at login-realbank-secure.com, and the device checks the origin, sees it doesn't match, and refuses to sign anything. A password or texted code typed into that same fake page works fine for the attacker; a FIDO2 credential simply does not.

SMS codes can be intercepted through SIM swapping or SS7 attacks, and both SMS and push-based MFA share a deeper weakness: a user can be socially engineered into handing over a code or approving a push they didn't request, which is exactly how MFA-fatigue, or push-bombing, attacks work — firing repeated approval requests until a tired user taps approve. Passkeys remove that human decision point. A passkey, the consumer-friendly packaging of FIDO2, syncs across a user's devices via Apple, Google, or Microsoft, so there's nothing extra to carry and nothing to approve under pressure.

Next, Lesson 8 turns to identities with no human behind them at all — service accounts, API keys, managed identities, and workload identities — and why they need an entirely different authentication treatment than a person tapping Face ID or approving a push.
